Urgent antimicrobial therapy targeting *N. gonorrhoeae*, including coverage for possible cephalosporin resistance, is indicated — per current CDC guidelines (e.g., ceftriaxone 1–2 g IV daily, plus azithromycin 1 g PO ×1 dose, pending susceptibility). Sexual health evaluation, partner notification, and screening for other STIs (HIV, syphilis, chlamydia) are essential next steps.

Diagnostician:

[THOUGHT]  
This is a classic, laboratory-confirmed case of disseminated gonococcal infection (DGI) manifesting as gonococcal septic arthritis. The diagnosis rests on high-quality synovial fluid evidence: Gram stain showing intracellular Gram-negative diplococci (highly specific in the appropriate clinical context), PCR confirmation of *Neisseria gonorrhoeae* DNA, and definitive culture growth on selective medium (VCN chocolate agar). The acute monoarticular wrist arthritis with systemic inflammation (leukocytosis, markedly elevated CRP/ESR), absence of trauma, and prior migratory arthralgia (transient left knee pain) strongly support DGI over other causes of septic arthritis (e.g., *Staphylococcus aureus*, which typically presents with more indolent or severe local signs and rarely shows migratory symptoms). The negative blood cultures are expected in DGI — bacteremia is often brief and low-grade. The absence of dermatitis or tenosynovitis does not exclude DGI; these features are present in only ~50–75% of cases, and isolated septic arthritis is a well-documented, later-stage manifestation. No alternative diagnosis explains the combination of neutrophilic pleocytosis, intracellular Gram-negative diplococci on synovial Gram stain, and molecular/microbiologic confirmation of *N. gonorrhoeae*.

[EVIDENCE]  
• Acute onset left wrist pain for 3 days, worsening acutely this morning, without trauma.  
• Systemic symptoms: chills and malaise.  
• Prior transient left knee pain (resolved spontaneously), consistent with migratory arthralgia — a hallmark of DGI.  
• Synovial fluid WBC >50,000/μL with neutrophil predominance.  
• Synovial fluid Gram stain shows Gram-negative diplococci.  
• Synovial fluid PCR is positive for *Neisseria gonorrhoeae* DNA.  
• Synovial fluid culture isolates *N. gonorrhoeae* on VCN-supplemented chocolate agar.  
• Blood cultures are negative — consistent with typical DGI.  
• Leukocytosis (15,000/μL), markedly elevated CRP (128 mg/L), and ESR (62 mm/hr) confirm systemic inflammatory response.

[GAPS]  
• No documented sexual history, genital examination findings, or nucleic acid test (NAAT) results from urogenital (urethral/cervical) or extragenital (pharyngeal/rectal) sites — though not required to diagnose DGI, these would help characterize the primary portal of entry and guide partner management.  
• No assessment of tenosynovitis (e.g., tendon sheath swelling, pain with passive motion of digits) — a common co-feature in DGI but not essential for diagnosis.  
• No HIV or syphilis serology results — relevant for STI co-screening but not diagnostically necessary for DGI confirmation.

[DIAGNOSIS]  
Disseminated Gonococcal Infection with gonococcal septic arthritis of the left wrist.
